title: I tested Hisense's affordable RGB TV, and while it delivers solid picture quality and performance, it's not the OLED-killer I was looking for
byline: James DavidsonSocial Links NavigationTV Hardware Staff Writer, Home Entertainment
excerpt: The Hisense UR8 is one of the first affordable RGB mini-LED models available and while it improves over mini-LED in some areas, it fails to impress in key areas.
content_html:
The Hisense UR8 brings RGB mini-LED to a more affordable price point, delivering impressive backlight control, good sports performance, and a ton of gaming features. Unfortunately, its colors, arguably its main selling point, are disappointing, not providing the wow-factor I was looking for. While this is still a good evolution of mini-LED, the technology here still isn't an OLED killer yet.

Hisense UR8 review: Two-minute review

The Hisense UR8 is the first ‘affordable’ RGB TV on the market, and while it has a strong feature set and mostly good picture quality, the UR8 doesn't demonstrate the ‘OLED-killer’ status the RGB tech has been given. While it’s a good TV, it can’t count itself among the best TVs I've tested this year.

The UR8 has a good number of smart and AI features, as well as features for gaming. It also has four HDMI 2.1 ports, an anti-glare screen akin to Samsung’s own Glare Free screens, and comes equipped with Hisense’s Hi-View AI RGB processor.

Picture quality on the UR8 is good, but delivers some disappointments. It demonstrates excellent backlight control for an LED, backlit TV, as well as strong contrast, decent black levels, and crisp textures. Its motion is also good, even with out-of-the-box picture modes, though I did note some blurring at times.

However, as this is an RGB TV, its big selling point should be its colors, and while they are natural, and can appear punchy, they’re not as bold as I hoped for, especially given its ostensibly impressive test measurements (more on that below). While RGB is a step forward in some aspects for mini-LED, TVs using the technology still can’t compete with the best OLED TVs.

Sound quality is solid. The UR8 delivers some weighty bass, good accuracy and precise sound mapping, and delivers clear speech in movies and TV shows. The soundstage can sound narrow, however, and Dolby Atmos effects aren’t always clear. While the built-in sound is good for the most part, home theater fans will likely want to supplement it with one of the best soundbars.

Gaming is one of the UR8’s strengths. With four HDMI 2.1 ports, all kitted out for gaming, it supports up to 4K 180Hz and VRR. When actually playing games, the UR8 feels responsive and delivers a smooth experience. Getting a low input lag time does require adjustment of settings and the picture isn’t always perfect; but while it doesn’t beat the best gaming TVs, the UR8 is still good for gaming.

Value is a mixed bag with the UR8. The 65-inch model I tested launched for $1,999 / £2,299 / AU$2,495, and while prices are already dropping in the US, and it's great value in Australia, its price in the UK puts it in direct competition with some of the best OLED TVs, like the LG C6. While it does deliver good performance and features for the price in the US and Australia, the same isn’t true for the UK.

Hisense UR8 review: Features

  • RGB mini-LED panel
  • Four HDMI 2.1 ports, up to 180Hz refresh rate
  • Anti-glare screen

The Hisense UR8 is the first affordable RGB mini-LED TV to come onto the market, with the Hisense UR9 taking the flagship spot. The UR8 and UR9 are the first RGB mini-LEDs available in smaller sizes, after the tech's introduction in the Hisense 116UX last year. While the UR9 and UR8 are both significantly cheaper than the 116UX, the UR8 is the more affordable option of the two, although it is still pricier than some standard mini-LED.

RGB mini-LED has a similar setup to standard mini-LED, but instead of purely white LEDs within the TV’s backlight, there are red, blue and green LEDs, which are designed to produce bolder colors and higher brightness than a standard mini-LED in the same bracket. Hisense claims that RGB mini-LED can hit 100% of the BT.2020 color space (more on that below).

The UR8 comes equipped with an anti-glare screen, similar to Samsung’s Glare Free screens. It’s a matte screen designed to reduce distracting, mirror-like reflections, to make viewing in brighter conditions easier.

The UR8 is equipped with Hisense’s Hi-View AI Engine RGB processor, which is designed to help boost color performance, as well as offer AI picture and sound features.The UR8 supports both Dolby Vision and HDR10+ HDR formats, as well as the new Dolby Vision 2 format, though no content is currently available for this format at the time of writing. IMAX Enhanced is also supported.

The UR8 comes with a great list of gaming features, including four HDMI 2.1 ports which all support up to 4K 180Hz (up to 4K 120Hz for consoles), VRR including AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Dolby Vision and HDR10+ gaming, and ALLM. There’s also a game menu, where settings for brightness boosting can be adjusted.

For sound, there’s a Devialet-tuned, 2.1.2 channel speaker system, totaling 70W of power. Dolby Atmos and DTS: X are both supported, and there are a plethora of audio settings and preset modes to dig into.

Which smart TV system the UR8 uses depends on your region. In the US, you get Google TV, while in the UK and Australia the UR8 uses Hisense’s own VIDAA smart TV. As I’m based in the UK, I’ll be discussing VIDAA. It supports an extensive number of apps, including big hitters like Netflix and Prime Video, as well as BBC iPlayer and ITVX in the UK. It also supports Freely in the UK, which can be used to watch live, broadcast TV over Wi-Fi, without the need for satellite or antenna connections.

  • Features score: 4.5 / 5

Hisense UR8 review: Picture quality

  • Great backlight control
  • Effective anti-glare screen
  • Colors don’t live up to measurements

In terms of brightness, the UR8 hits some interesting numbers. In Filmmaker Mode, it hit a measured peak HDR brightness of 2,097 nits and in Standard, it hit 2,394 nits. These are solid results, and while flagship OLEDs such as the Samsung S99H are now beating this (it hits 2,743 nits peak HDR), it does beat more standard mini-LEDs in its price bracket such as the Samsung QN80H, which I measured at 1,149 nits peak HDR (though this was on the 55-inch model).

Fullscreen HDR brightness is also solid, clocking in at 771 nits and 767 nits in Filmmaker and Standard modes respectively. Where the UR8 delivers more impressive brightness is in SDR Standard, where it hit a peak of 1,514 nits and fullscreen of 778.

The most surprising measurement, though, was the UR8’s HDR color gamut coverage. Not only did it hit 95.1% of the BT.2020 color space, the highest I’ve measured on a TV to date, but it registered a staggering 145.2% of the UHDA-P3 color space, which massively exceeds the high of 100% I registered on the Samsung S95F last year with the same color space.

Looking at these results, I expected colors to be spectacular — and this brings me to my main criticism of the UR8: the colors I saw did not reflect those measurements. When I watched Elemental, the UR8 still delivered punchy, vibrant colors such as Ember’s flame and the blue of Wade’s water, but they didn’t have the pop I was expecting. In La La Land, at the Spring party, Mia’s yellow dress is bright and natural looking, but I’d seen more engaging colors on other TVs.

I found when I compared the UR8 to the Samsung QN80H, a standard mini-LED in the same price range, the QN80H actually delivered bolder colors. Taking the same La La Land scene for comparison, Mia’s yellow dress, the green bushes, and the red outfits of some party-goers all looked much more vibrant on the QN80H. The UR8’s colors looked natural, but lacked that wow factor I expected from an RGB TV.

It was a shame the UR8’s colors weren’t as dazzling as I’d hoped, because in other areas, the UR8 shines, especially its backlight control. Standard mini-LED TVs can really suffer from blooming (where light from a bright object against a dark background can create a halo effect around said object), but this wasn’t the case with the UR8, which demonstrated little to no blooming through most tests. Watching the UR8 at more extreme angles did reveal some blooming, but it was better than what I’ve seen on some mini-LED TVs in the past.

Watching The Batman, the UR8 demonstrated solid contrast too, with mostly deep black tones and a good balance between light and dark tones, shown as Batman wanders around the crime scene at Mayor Mithcell’s home, or in the bright lights around the Batcave. I did notice blacks could take on a gray hue in some scenes, but for the most part, The Batman looked good.

I did find that the Dolby Vision Dark picture mode was too dim to watch in a bright room, despite the anti-reflection screen, but worked well in ambient and dimmer conditions. The brighter Dolby Vision IQ picture mode works best for brighter rooms. If you do use Dolby Vision IQ, I recommend dropping the brightness from 50 to 49 and turning off precision detail and super resolution for a more natural-looking image with better contrast.

It was a similar story with Alien: Romulus. The UR8 did a solid job displaying the scenes in space, with good contrast between the light from the moon and the black of space as the crew approached the Renaissance station. The black of space was occasionally gray, but still very good for a mini-LED, backlit TV. Again, backlight control proved to be the UR8’s strong suit.

In all HDR movies, the UR8 delivered crisp textures, with refined detail in people, clothing and objects. The UR8 did a good job showing the intricate textures of the various consoles onboard the mining ship in Alien: Romulus. Close-up shots showed sweat, hairs, and facial details like wrinkles with real clarity as well.

One thing I did find odd was that for non-Dolby Vision content, the Filmmaker, Movie, and IMAX Enhanced picture modes all looked identical. There seemed to be no real difference in brightness, color or contrast — something I would expect from a TV.

The UR8 did a good job with sports. Watching some World Cup highlights on BBC iPlayer, motion was smooth in the default Sports picture mode. While most of the motion styles worked, I found myself using either Clear or Standard. Color enhancer is on by default in this mode, and I personally found the colors too oversaturated, so I turned this off, and colors looked more natural. I did notice there was muddying of textures during very quick camera pans, but for the most part, the UR8 worked well for sports.

  • Picture quality score: 4 / 5

Hisense UR8 review: Sound quality

  • 2.1.2 channel speaker array
  • Good bass and accuracy
  • Soundstage can be narrow

The UR8 has a built-in 2.1.2 channel speaker array, tuned by Devialet, with a total power of 70W. There are a good number of preset sound modes and settings, but I mainly used Standard and Theater mode for my testing.

Watching the Penguin chase scene from The Batman, the UR8 delivered good bass levels, accurately conveying the loud rumble of the Batmobile’s engine. The UR8 demonstrated good accuracy too, mapping the sound of swerving tires, bullet sprays and the horns of passing traffic to the action on screen with solid precision.

While I typically use Theater mode on most TVs, I found that the UR8’s could get harsh at times, with a sudden brightness that I found distracting. Standard mode was a more than suitable alternative, and although it didn't have as wide a sound field as Theater mode, it was more controlled.

The UR8 delivers solid sound overall, but I did feel its soundstage was narrow, meaning not every element of The Batman scene was given room to breathe. It’s a decent sound system for a TV, but overall I’d still recommend a soundbar to go with it.

  • Sound quality score: 4 / 5

Hisense UR8 review: Design

  • Sturdy build
  • Solid pedestal stand
  • Slightly bulkier depth

The UR8 has a functional, safe design. The TV itself feels sturdy when installed on its central pedestal stand, which does feel solid even though it’s made of a plastic material. The TV is slighter deeper than some rivals, such as the Samsung QN80H, but again it feels well built.

As I mentioned above, the UR8 features an anti-glare screen, which does a good job of limiting reflections in brighter conditions. The 65-inch model I tested felt light for its size and it has a trim bezel, although the bottom bezel is thicker than those on the top and sides. Connections are easily accessible on the side of the rear of the TV.

The UR8 comes with Hisense’s own USB-C and solar rechargeable remote, which for me is one of the better controllers on the market. It does feel a bit light, but for me the button layout is logical, and it’s nice to see a rechargeable remote supplied with a cheaper TV.

  • Design score: 4 / 5

Hisense UR8 review: Smart TV & menus

  • Google TV US, VIDAA UK and Australia
  • Good number of picture and audio settings
  • Dated appearance

As I’m based in the UK, I’ll be discussing the VIDAA smart TV platform featured in the UR8 (also used in Australian models). If you’re based in the US, the UR8 uses Google TV as its smart TV platform instead.

VIDAA is a serviceable smart TV system. It supports a good number of major apps including Netflix, Disney Plus and Prime Video, as well apps from UK broadcasters, including BBC iPlayer and ITVX. The home screen offers a lot of content recommendations, but there's also a large banner space at the top of the screen for ads, which can be distracting.

The menus are neatly and logically laid out, with most settings easy to find. Response times when navigating these menus is good too. There are plenty of settings for adjusting both the picture and sound, although I didn’t use a lot of them.

VIDAA does, however, look a little dated, especially in the menus. It doesn’t have the sleekness of Samsung’s Tizen or Google TV, or the simplicity and color of Roku. Secondly, as someone who does change settings a lot, a pop-up eco warning appears every time and this can get frustrating; and there seems to be no way to turn it off.

  • Smart TV score: 3.5 or 4

Hisense UR8 review: Gaming

  • Near-full suite of features
  • 11.7ms input lag (with the right settings)
  • Up to 4K 180Hz refresh rate supported

The UR8 is actually very well equipped for gaming. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports that support 4K up to 180Hz (4K 120Hz for consoles is supported), VRR including FreeSync Premium Pro, both Dolby Vision and HDR10+ gaming, and ALLM.

To get the lowest input lag time, which I measured at 11.7ms in 4K 60Hz, you do have to mess around with some settings. Having put the UR8 into Game mode, I then had to turn on a refresh rate feature, which prioritized faster frame rates, and this is how I got the above result. Without adjusting those settings I measured the input lag time at 20ms, above the 15ms threshold we look for in testing.

Playing Battlefield V in 4K 120Hz, actual gameplay felt smooth, and the UR8 did a good job handling fast-moving action sequences like a shootout in a desert mission. The overall picture quality was good, with high brightness, bold color and solid contrast. I did notice that, during particularly quick camera pans, some textures could muddy, but this didn’t happen every time.

  • Gaming score: 4.5 / 5

Hisense UR8 review: Value

  • Great value in the US and Australia
  • Overpriced in the UK
  • Overall good performance for the price

Value is a tough attribute to grade for the Hisense UR8. As RGB mini-LED is still in its infancy (having only been introduced in 2025, and only come to smaller screens for the first time this year), I did anticipate that RGB TVs would be pricey, even more entry-level models like the UR8.

With the UR8, it all comes down to where you are. When it's on sale, you can pick the 65-inch model up for $1,499 in the US, and prices are only going to drop. This puts the UR8 in direct competition price-wise with standard mini-LED, giving people looking for a TV within that price range more choice. It's also good value in Australia, with the 65-inch launching for AU$2,495, which translates to $1,799 / £1,299. I expect prices in Australia to come down reasonably quickly too.

The same can’t be said for the UK, unfortunately. The 65-inch launched recently at £2,299, which is actually pricier than the LG C6 OLED — and while RGB is meant to be a direct rival to OLED, as I've mentioned, it’s not there yet. I have seen the UR8 drop to £1,999 at some retailers, but this is still OLED-level pricing.

Overall, the UR8 does deliver pretty good value for money. It’s got a good feature set, delivers decent built-in sound, and is good for gaming, and while the picture doesn’t quite deliver what I’d hoped for, it’s still solid compared to most mini-LED. It’s just a shame that the value proposition is region-dependent.

  • Value score: 4 / 5

How I tested the Hisense UR8

  • Tested over two weeks
  • Tested in different lighting conditions in lab
  • Measurements taken using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software

My first step in testing the Hisense UR8 was to establish the best picture modes for critical testing, and I landed on Filmmaker Mode and Cinema mode (which admittedly looked very similar).

I then used reference scenes to test the UR8's picture quality, focusing on brightness, color, detail, upscaling, contrast and backlight control. I used a couple of these same scenes to test the TV's built-in speakers.

I also used an Xbox Series X to test the TV's gaming features and performance, playing Battlefield V.

Apart from objective testing, I took measurements of the UR8 using specialized equipment. This included a Jeti Spctral 15VA Spectroradiometer and Klein K-10A colorimeter (with both meters profiled together), with a Murideo Six G 8K Metal test-pattern generator. I took measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.

The first measurements I took were the UR8's brightness, in both SDR and HDR. I used white window patterns in sizes ranging from 1-100%, with peak (10%) and fullscreen (100%) windows serving as the primary focus. I took measurements in the UR8's Standard and Filmmaker Mode pictures modes.

After this, I measured the color and grayscale accuracy (in SDR), focusing on the Delta-E values (the margin for error between the test signal sent and what's displayed on screen).

Next, I measured the UR8's HDR color gamut coverage, focusing on the BT.2020 and UHDA-P3 color spaces.

I also measured the UR8's HDR EOTF in 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits. This shows the UR8 accuracy at both light and dark levels. I also tested the UR8's spectral power distribution, which demonstrates color performance.

Finally, I tested the UR8's input lag time using a Leo Bodnar 4K HDMi Input Lag Tester.

The UR8 and UR9 are the first RGB mini-LEDs available in smaller sizes, after the tech's introduction in the Hisense 116UX last year. While the UR9 and UR8 are both significantly cheaper than the 116UX, the UR8 is the more affordable option of the two, although it is still pricier than some standard mini-LED.RGB mini-LED has a similar setup to standard mini-LED, but instead of purely white LEDs within the TV’s backlight, there are red, blue and green LEDs, which are designed to produce bolder colors and higher brightness than a standard mini-LED in the same bracket. Hisense claims that RGB mini-LED can hit 100% of the BT.2020 color space (more on that below).The UR8 comes equipped with an anti-glare screen, similar to Samsung’s Glare Free screens. It’s a matte screen designed to reduce distracting, mirror-like reflections, to make viewing in brighter conditions easier.The UR8 is equipped with Hisense’s Hi-View AI Engine RGB processor, which is designed to help boost color performance, as well as offer AI picture and sound features.The UR8 supports both Dolby Vision and HDR10+ HDR formats, as well as the new Dolby Vision 2 format, though no content is currently available for this format at the time of writing. IMAX Enhanced is also supported.The UR8 comes with a great list of gaming features, including four HDMI 2.1 ports which all support up to 4K 180Hz (up to 4K 120Hz for consoles), VRR including AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Dolby Vision and HDR10+ gaming, and ALLM. There’s also a game menu, where settings for brightness boosting can be adjusted.For sound, there’s a Devialet-tuned, 2.1.2 channel speaker system, totaling 70W of power. Dolby Atmos and DTS: X are both supported, and there are a plethora of audio settings and preset modes to dig into.Which smart TV system the UR8 uses depends on your region. In the US, you get Google TV, while in the UK and Australia the UR8 uses Hisense’s own VIDAA smart TV. As I’m based in the UK, I’ll be discussing VIDAA. It supports an extensive number of apps, including big hitters like Netflix and Prime Video, as well as BBC iPlayer and ITVX in the UK. It also supports Freely in the UK, which can be used to watch live, broadcast TV over Wi-Fi, without the need for satellite or antenna connections.Features score: 4.5 / 5Hisense UR8 review: Picture quality The UR8 delivers some vibrant colors (shown here in a scene from Elemental), but they seem lacking for RGB (Image credit: Disney / Future)Great backlight control Effective anti-glare screenColors don’t live up to measurementsIn terms of brightness, the UR8 hits some interesting numbers. In Filmmaker Mode, it hit a measured peak HDR brightness of 2,097 nits and in Standard, it hit 2,394 nits. These are solid results, and while flagship OLEDs such as the Samsung S99H are now beating this (it hits 2,743 nits peak HDR), it does beat more standard mini-LEDs in its price bracket such as the Samsung QN80H, which I measured at 1,149 nits peak HDR (though this was on the 55-inch model).Fullscreen HDR brightness is also solid, clocking in at 771 nits and 767 nits in Filmmaker and Standard modes respectively. Where the UR8 delivers more impressive brightness is in SDR Standard, where it hit a peak of 1,514 nits and fullscreen of 778.The most surprising measurement, though, was the UR8’s HDR color gamut coverage. Not only did it hit 95.1% of the BT.2020 color space, the highest I’ve measured on a TV to date, but it registered a staggering 145.2% of the UHDA-P3 color space, which massively exceeds the high of 100% I registered on the Samsung S95F last year with the same color space.Looking at these results, I expected colors to be spectacular — and this brings me to my main criticism of the UR8: the colors I saw did not reflect those measurements. When I watched Elemental, the UR8 still delivered punchy, vibrant colors such as Ember’s flame and the blue of Wade’s water, but they didn’t have the pop I was expecting. In La La Land, at the Spring party, Mia’s yellow dress is bright and natural looking, but I’d seen more engaging colors on other TVs.I found when I compared the UR8 to the Samsung QN80H, a standard mini-LED in the same price range, the QN80H actually delivered bolder colors. Taking the same La La Land scene for comparison, Mia’s yellow dress, the green bushes, and the red outfits of some party-goers all looked much more vibrant on the QN80H. The UR8’s colors looked natural, but lacked that wow factor I expected from an RGB TV. The UR8 has some of the best backlight control I've seen from a mini-LED TV (Image credit: Warner Bros. / Future)It was a shame the UR8’s colors weren’t as dazzling as I’d hoped, because in other areas, the UR8 shines, especially its backlight control. Standard mini-LED TVs can really suffer from blooming (where light from a bright object against a dark background can create a halo effect around said object), but this wasn’t the case with the UR8, which demonstrated little to no blooming through most tests. Watching the UR8 at more extreme angles did reveal some blooming, but it was better than what I’ve seen on some mini-LED TVs in the past.Watching The Batman, the UR8 demonstrated solid contrast too, with mostly deep black tones and a good balance between light and dark tones, shown as Batman wanders around the crime scene at Mayor Mithcell’s home, or in the bright lights around the Batcave. I did notice blacks could take on a gray hue in some scenes, but for the most part, The Batman looked good.I did find that the Dolby Vision Dark picture mode was too dim to watch in a bright room, despite the anti-reflection screen, but worked well in ambient and dimmer conditions. The brighter Dolby Vision IQ picture mode works best for brighter rooms. If you do use Dolby Vision IQ, I recommend dropping the brightness from 50 to 49 and turning off precision detail and super resolution for a more natural-looking image with better contrast.It was a similar story with Alien: Romulus. The UR8 did a solid job displaying the scenes in space, with good contrast between the light from the moon and the black of space as the crew approached the Renaissance station. The black of space was occasionally gray, but still very good for a mini-LED, backlit TV. Again, backlight control proved to be the UR8’s strong suit. Textures and details appear crisp in most movies, seen here in La La Land (Image credit: Future)In all HDR movies, the UR8 delivered crisp textures, with refined detail in people, clothing and objects. The UR8 did a good job showing the intricate textures of the various consoles onboard the mining ship in Alien: Romulus. Close-up shots showed sweat, hairs, and facial details like wrinkles with real clarity as well.One thing I did find odd was that for non-Dolby Vision content, the Filmmaker, Movie, and IMAX Enhanced picture modes all looked identical. There seemed to be no real difference in brightness, color or contrast — something I would expect from a TV.The UR8 did a good job with sports. Watching some World Cup highlights on BBC iPlayer, motion was smooth in the default Sports picture mode. While most of the motion styles worked, I found myself using either Clear or Standard. Color enhancer is on by default in this mode, and I personally found the colors too oversaturated, so I turned this off, and colors looked more natural. I did notice there was muddying of textures during very quick camera pans, but for the most part, the UR8 worked well for sports.Picture quality score: 4 / 5Hisense UR8 review: Sound quality The UR8 delivers solid overall built-in sound (Image credit: Warner Bros. / Future)2.1.2 channel speaker array Good bass and accuracy Soundstage can be narrowThe UR8 has a built-in 2.1.2 channel speaker array, tuned by Devialet, with a total power of 70W. There are a good number of preset sound modes and settings, but I mainly used Standard and Theater mode for my testing.Watching the Penguin chase scene from The Batman, the UR8 delivered good bass levels, accurately conveying the loud rumble of the Batmobile’s engine. The UR8 demonstrated good accuracy too, mapping the sound of swerving tires, bullet sprays and the horns of passing traffic to the action on screen with solid precision.While I typically use Theater mode on most TVs, I found that the UR8’s could get harsh at times, with a sudden brightness that I found distracting. Standard mode was a more than suitable alternative, and although it didn't have as wide a sound field as Theater mode, it was more controlled.The UR8 delivers solid sound overall, but I did feel its soundstage was narrow, meaning not every element of The Batman scene was given room to breathe. It’s a decent sound system for a TV, but overall I’d still recommend a soundbar to go with it.Sound quality score: 4 / 5Hisense UR8 review: Design The UR8 has a safe, solid design, and uses a central pedestal stand (Image credit: Future)Sturdy build Solid pedestal stand Slightly bulkier depthThe UR8 has a functional, safe design. The TV itself feels sturdy when installed on its central pedestal stand, which does feel solid even though it’s made of a plastic material. The TV is slighter deeper than some rivals, such as the Samsung QN80H, but again it feels well built.As I mentioned above, the UR8 features an anti-glare screen, which does a good job of limiting reflections in brighter conditions. The 65-inch model I tested felt light for its size and it has a trim bezel, although the bottom bezel is thicker than those on the top and sides. Connections are easily accessible on the side of the rear of the TV.The UR8 comes with Hisense’s own USB-C and solar rechargeable remote, which for me is one of the better controllers on the market. It does feel a bit light, but for me the button layout is logical, and it’s nice to see a rechargeable remote supplied with a cheaper TV.Design score: 4 / 5Hisense UR8 review: Smart TV & menus Your smart TV will vary depending on region. The UR8 uses Google TV in the US and VIDAA (home screen pictured) in the UK and Australia. (Image credit: Future)Google TV US, VIDAA UK and AustraliaGood number of picture and audio settings Dated appearance As I’m based in the UK, I’ll be discussing the VIDAA smart TV platform featured in the UR8 (also used in Australian models). If you’re based in the US, the UR8 uses Google TV as its smart TV platform instead.VIDAA is a serviceable smart TV system. It supports a good number of major apps including Netflix, Disney Plus and Prime Video, as well apps from UK broadcasters, including BBC iPlayer and ITVX. The home screen offers a lot of content recommendations, but there's also a large banner space at the top of the screen for ads, which can be distracting.The menus are neatly and logically laid out, with most settings easy to find. Response times when navigating these menus is good too. There are plenty of settings for adjusting both the picture and sound, although I didn’t use a lot of them.VIDAA does, however, look a little dated, especially in the menus. It doesn’t have the sleekness of Samsung’s Tizen or Google TV, or the simplicity and color of Roku. Secondly, as someone who does change settings a lot, a pop-up eco warning appears every time and this can get frustrating; and there seems to be no way to turn it off.Smart TV score: 3.5 or 4Hisense UR8 review: Gaming The UR8 has an excellent choice of gaming features, and delivers solid gaming performance (Image credit: Future)Near-full suite of features11.7ms input lag (with the right settings)Up to 4K 180Hz refresh rate supportedThe UR8 is actually very well equipped for gaming. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports that support 4K up to 180Hz (4K 120Hz for consoles is supported), VRR including FreeSync Premium Pro, both Dolby Vision and HDR10+ gaming, and ALLM.To get the lowest input lag time, which I measured at 11.7ms in 4K 60Hz, you do have to mess around with some settings. Having put the UR8 into Game mode, I then had to turn on a refresh rate feature, which prioritized faster frame rates, and this is how I got the above result. Without adjusting those settings I measured the input lag time at 20ms, above the 15ms threshold we look for in testing.Playing Battlefield V in 4K 120Hz, actual gameplay felt smooth, and the UR8 did a good job handling fast-moving action sequences like a shootout in a desert mission. The overall picture quality was good, with high brightness, bold color and solid contrast. I did notice that, during particularly quick camera pans, some textures could muddy, but this didn’t happen every time.Gaming score: 4.5 / 5Hisense UR8 review: Value (Image credit: Future)Great value in the US and AustraliaOverpriced in the UK Overall good performance for the priceValue is a tough attribute to grade for the Hisense UR8. As RGB mini-LED is still in its infancy (having only been introduced in 2025, and only come to smaller screens for the first time this year), I did anticipate that RGB TVs would be pricey, even more entry-level models like the UR8.With the UR8, it all comes down to where you are. When it's on sale, you can pick the 65-inch model up for $1,499 in the US, and prices are only going to drop. This puts the UR8 in direct competition price-wise with standard mini-LED, giving people looking for a TV within that price range more choice. It's also good value in Australia, with the 65-inch launching for AU$2,495, which translates to $1,799 / £1,299. I expect prices in Australia to come down reasonably quickly too.The same can’t be said for the UK, unfortunately. The 65-inch launched recently at £2,299, which is actually pricier than the LG C6 OLED — and while RGB is meant to be a direct rival to OLED, as I've mentioned, it’s not there yet. I have seen the UR8 drop to £1,999 at some retailers, but this is still OLED-level pricing.Overall, the UR8 does deliver pretty good value for money. It’s got a good feature set, delivers decent built-in sound, and is good for gaming, and while the picture doesn’t quite deliver what I’d hoped for, it’s still solid compared to most mini-LED. It’s just a shame that the value proposition is region-dependent.Value score: 4 / 5Should you buy the Hisense UR8? I used a couple of these same scenes to test the TV's built-in speakers.I also used an Xbox Series X to test the TV's gaming features and performance, playing Battlefield V.Apart from objective testing, I took measurements of the UR8 using specialized equipment. This included a Jeti Spctral 15VA Spectroradiometer and Klein K-10A colorimeter (with both meters profiled together), with a Murideo Six G 8K Metal test-pattern generator. I took measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.The first measurements I took were the UR8's brightness, in both SDR and HDR. I used white window patterns in sizes ranging from 1-100%, with peak (10%) and fullscreen (100%) windows serving as the primary focus. I took measurements in the UR8's Standard and Filmmaker Mode pictures modes.After this, I measured the color and grayscale accuracy (in SDR), focusing on the Delta-E values (the margin for error between the test signal sent and what's displayed on screen).Next, I measured the UR8's HDR color gamut coverage, focusing on the BT.2020 and UHDA-P3 color spaces.I also measured the UR8's HDR EOTF in 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits. blocks.html_en: The Hisense UR8 is the first affordable RGB mini-LED TV to come onto the market, with the Hisense UR9 taking the flagship spot. The UR8 and UR9 are the first RGB mini-LEDs available in smaller sizes, after the tech's introduction in the Hisense 116UX last year. While the UR9 and UR8 are both significantly cheaper than the 116UX, the UR8 is the more affordable option of the two, although it is still pricier than some standard mini-LED.

Hisense claims that RGB mini-LED can hit 100% of the BT.2020 color space (more on that below).

IMAX Enhanced is also supported.

There’s also a game menu, where settings for brightness boosting can be adjusted.

It also supports Freely in the UK, which can be used to watch live, broadcast TV over Wi-Fi, without the need for satellite or antenna connections.

blocks.html_en: In terms of brightness, the UR8 hits some interesting numbers. In Filmmaker Mode, it hit a measured peak HDR brightness of 2,097 nits and in Standard, it hit 2,394 nits. These are solid results, and while flagship OLEDs such as the Samsung S99H are now beating this (it hits 2,743 nits peak HDR), it does beat more standard mini-LEDs in its price bracket such as the Samsung QN80H, which I measured at 1,149 nits peak HDR (though this was on the 55-inch model).

sentences.zh: 这些都是可靠的结果，虽然三星 S99H 等旗舰 OLED 现在已经击败了这一点（它达到了 2,743 尼特峰值 HDR），但它确实击败了同价位的更多标准 mini-LED，例如三星 QN80H，我测得它的峰值 HDR 为 1,149 尼特（尽管这是在 55 英寸型号上）。

blocks.html_en: Fullscreen HDR brightness is also solid, clocking in at 771 nits and 767 nits in Filmmaker and Standard modes respectively. Where the UR8 delivers more impressive brightness is in SDR Standard, where it hit a peak of 1,514 nits and fullscreen of 778.

blocks.html_en: The most surprising measurement, though, was the UR8’s HDR color gamut coverage. Not only did it hit 95.1% of the BT.2020 color space, the highest I’ve measured on a TV to date, but it registered a staggering 145.2% of the UHDA-P3 color space, which massively exceeds the high of 100% I registered on the Samsung S95F last year with the same color space.

sentences.en: Not only did it hit 95.1% of the BT.2020 color space, the highest I’ve measured on a TV to date, but it registered a staggering 145.2% of the UHDA-P3 color space, which massively exceeds the high of 100% I registered on the Samsung S95F last year with the same color space.
sentences.zh: 它不仅达到了 BT.2020 色彩空间的 95.1%，这是我迄今为止在电视上测得的最高值，而且它在 UHDA-P3 色彩空间中的色彩空间达到了惊人的 145.2%，这大大超过了我去年在三星 S95F 上使用相同色彩空间时所达到的 100% 的高点。

blocks.html_en: Looking at these results, I expected colors to be spectacular — and this brings me to my main criticism of the UR8: the colors I saw did not reflect those measurements. When I watched Elemental, the UR8 still delivered punchy, vibrant colors such as Ember’s flame and the blue of Wade’s water, but they didn’t have the pop I was expecting. In La La Land, at the Spring party, Mia’s yellow dress is bright and natural looking, but I’d seen more engaging colors on other TVs.

blocks.html_en: I found when I compared the UR8 to the Samsung QN80H, a standard mini-LED in the same price range, the QN80H actually delivered bolder colors. Taking the same La La Land scene for comparison, Mia’s yellow dress, the green bushes, and the red outfits of some party-goers all looked much more vibrant on the QN80H. The UR8’s colors looked natural, but lacked that wow factor I expected from an RGB TV.

sentences.en: The UR8 has some of the best backlight control I've seen from a mini-LED TV (Image credit: Warner Bros. / Future)

blocks.html_en: It was a shame the UR8’s colors weren’t as dazzling as I’d hoped, because in other areas, the UR8 shines, especially its backlight control. Standard mini-LED TVs can really suffer from blooming (where light from a bright object against a dark background can create a halo effect around said object), but this wasn’t the case with the UR8, which demonstrated little to no blooming through most tests. Watching the UR8 at more extreme angles did reveal some blooming, but it was better than what I’ve seen on some mini-LED TVs in the past.

sentences.en: It was a shame the UR8’s colors weren’t as dazzling as I’d hoped, because in other areas, the UR8 shines, especially its backlight control.

sentences.en: Standard mini-LED TVs can really suffer from blooming (where light from a bright object against a dark background can create a halo effect around said object), but this wasn’t the case with the UR8, which demonstrated little to no blooming through most tests.

I did notice blacks could take on a gray hue in some scenes, but for the most part, The Batman looked good.

sentences.zh: 在观看《蝙蝠侠》时，UR8 也表现出了强烈的对比度，以深黑色调为主，明暗色调之间保持着良好的平衡，表现出蝙蝠侠在米斯塞尔市长家的犯罪现场或蝙蝠洞周围的明亮灯光下徘徊。

blocks.html_en: I did find that the Dolby Vision Dark picture mode was too dim to watch in a bright room, despite the anti-reflection screen, but worked well in ambient and dimmer conditions. The brighter Dolby Vision IQ picture mode works best for brighter rooms. If you do use Dolby Vision IQ, I recommend dropping the brightness from 50 to 49 and turning off precision detail and super resolution for a more natural-looking image with better contrast.

blocks.html_en: In all HDR movies, the UR8 delivered crisp textures, with refined detail in people, clothing and objects. sentences.zh: UR8 很好地展示了《异形：罗慕路斯》中采矿船上各种控制台的复杂纹理。

blocks.html_en: One thing I did find odd was that for non-Dolby Vision content, the Filmmaker, Movie, and IMAX Enhanced picture modes all looked identical. There seemed to be no real difference in brightness, color or contrast — something I would expect from a TV.

sentences.en: There seemed to be no real difference in brightness, color or contrast — something I would expect from a TV.
sentences.zh: 亮度、颜色或对比度似乎没有真正的差异——这是我对电视的期望。

blocks.html_en: The UR8 did a good job with sports. Watching some World Cup highlights on BBC iPlayer, motion was smooth in the default Sports picture mode. sentences.zh: UR8 提供稳定的整体内置声音（图片来源：Warner Bros./Future）

sentences.zh: UR8 具有安全、坚固的设计，并使用中央底座（图片来源：Future）

blocks.html_en: To get the lowest input lag time, which I measured at 11.7ms in 4K 60Hz, you do have to mess around with some settings. blocks.html_en: Value is a tough attribute to grade for the Hisense UR8. blocks.html_en: My first step in testing the Hisense UR8 was to establish the best picture modes for critical testing, and I landed on Filmmaker Mode and Cinema mode (which admittedly looked very similar).

sentences.en: My first step in testing the Hisense UR8 was to establish the best picture modes for critical testing, and I landed on Filmmaker Mode and Cinema mode (which admittedly looked very similar).

blocks.html_en: I then used reference scenes to test the UR8's picture quality, focusing on brightness, color, detail, upscaling, contrast and backlight control. I used a couple of these same scenes to test the TV's built-in speakers.

I took measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.

sentences.en: This included a Jeti Spctral 15VA Spectroradiometer and Klein K-10A colorimeter (with both meters profiled together), with a Murideo Six G 8K Metal test-pattern generator.
sentences.zh: 其中包括 Jeti Spctral 15VA 光谱辐射计和 Klein K-10A 色度计（两种仪表一起配置），以及 Murideo Six G 8K Metal 测试图案生成器。

sentences.en: I took measurements using Portrait Displays' Calman color calibration software.

blocks.html_en: The first measurements I took were the UR8's brightness, in both SDR and HDR. sentences.en: The first measurements I took were the UR8's brightness, in both SDR and HDR.

sentences.en: I took measurements in the UR8's Standard and Filmmaker Mode pictures modes.
sentences.zh: 我在 UR8 的标准和电影制作模式图片模式下进行了测量。

blocks.html_en: After this, I measured the color and grayscale accuracy (in SDR), focusing on the Delta-E values (the margin for error between the test signal sent and what's displayed on screen).

sentences.en: After this, I measured the color and grayscale accuracy (in SDR), focusing on the Delta-E values (the margin for error between the test signal sent and what's displayed on screen).

blocks.html_en: Next, I measured the UR8's HDR color gamut coverage, focusing on the BT.2020 and UHDA-P3 color spaces.

blocks.html_en: I also measured the UR8's HDR EOTF in 1,000, 4,000 and 10,000 nits. This shows the UR8 accuracy at both light and dark levels. I also tested the UR8's spectral power distribution, which demonstrates color performance.

海信 UR8 将 RGB mini-LED 带到了更实惠的价格点，提供令人印象深刻的背光控制、良好的运动性能和大量的游戏功能。 不幸的是，它的颜色（可以说是它的主要卖点）令人失望，没有提供我一直在寻找的令人惊叹的因素。 虽然这仍然是 mini-LED 的一个很好的发展，但该技术仍然不是 OLED 杀手。

Pros

  • +出色的背光控制
  • +良好的游戏功能和性能
  • +有效防眩光屏幕

Cons

  • - 真实世界的颜色与测量值不符
  • - 电影画面模式几乎没有变化
  • - 快节奏动作中的一些纹理模糊

海信UR8评测：两分钟评测

海信 UR8 是市场上第一款“价格实惠”的 RGB 电视，虽然它具有强大的功能集和良好的图像质量，但 UR8 并没有表现出 RGB 技术所赋予的“OLED 杀手”地位。 虽然它是一台好电视，但它并不能算作我今年测试过的最好的电视之一。

UR8 拥有大量智能和人工智能功能，以及游戏功能。 它还具有四个 HDMI 2.1 端口、类似于三星自己的防眩光屏幕的防眩光屏幕，并配备了海信的 Hi-View AI RGB 处理器。

UR8 的图像质量很好，但也有些令人失望。 它展示了 LED 背光电视的出色背光控制，以及强烈的对比度、良好的黑色水平和清晰的纹理。 即使在开箱即用的图片模式下，它的运动也很好，尽管我有时确实注意到一些模糊。

然而，由于这是一台 RGB 电视，它的最大卖点应该是它的颜色，虽然它们很自然，而且看起来很有冲击力，但它们并不像我希望的那么大胆，特别是考虑到它表面上令人印象深刻的测试测量（更多内容见下文）。 虽然 RGB 在某些方面比 mini-LED 向前迈出了一步，但使用该技术的电视仍然无法与最好的 OLED 电视竞争。

音质很扎实。 UR8 提供厚重的低音、良好的准确性和精确的声音映射，并在电影和电视节目中提供清晰的语音。 然而，声场听起来很狭窄，而且杜比全景声 (Dolby Atmos) 效果并不总是清晰。 虽然内置声音在大多数情况下都很好，但家庭影院爱好者可能会希望用最好的条形音箱之一来补充它。

游戏是 UR8 的优势之一。 它具有四个 HDMI 2.1 端口，全部专为游戏而设计，支持高达 4K 180Hz 和 VRR。 实际玩游戏时，UR8感觉反应灵敏，体验流畅。 获得较低的输入延迟时间确实需要调整设置，并且图像并不总是完美的；虽然 UR8 无法击败最好的游戏电视，但它仍然非常适合游戏。

UR8 的价值是一个混合体。 我测试的 65 英寸型号的售价为 1,999 美元/2,299 英镑/2,495 澳元，虽然美国的价格已经在下降，而且在澳大利亚也很有价值，但它在英国的价格使其与一些最好的 OLED 电视（如 LG C6）直接竞争。 虽然它在美国和澳大利亚的价格上确实提供了良好的性能和功能，但在英国却并非如此。

海信UR8评测：特点

  • RGB 迷你 LED 面板
  • 四个 HDMI 2.1 端口，刷新率高达 180Hz
  • 防眩光屏幕

海信 UR8 是市场上第一款价格实惠的 RGB mini LED 电视，海信 UR9 占据旗舰位置。 继去年海信 116UX 引入该技术后，UR8 和 UR9 是首款尺寸更小的 RGB mini-LED。 虽然 UR9 和 UR8 都比 116UX 便宜得多，但 UR8 是两者中更实惠的选择，尽管它仍然比一些标准 mini-LED 贵。

RGB mini-LED 的设置与标准 mini-LED 类似，但电视背光中不是纯白色 LED，而是红色、蓝色和绿色 LED，其设计目的是比同一支架中的标准 mini-LED 产生更大胆的色彩和更高的亮度。 海信声称 RGB mini-LED 可以达到 100% 的 BT.2020 色彩空间（更多内容见下文）。

UR8 配备了防眩光屏幕，类似于三星的防眩光屏幕。 它是一款哑光屏幕，旨在减少分散注意力的镜面反射，使在明亮条件下观看更容易。

UR8 配备海信 Hi-View AI Engine RGB 处理器，旨在帮助提升色彩性能，并提供 AI 图像和声音功能。UR8 支持杜比视界和 HDR10+ HDR 格式，以及新的杜比视界 2 格式，但在撰写本文时，目前还没有该格式的内容。 还支持 IMAX 增强版。

UR8 配备了一系列出色的游戏功能，包括四个 HDMI 2.1 端口，全部支持高达 4K 180Hz（游戏机高达 4K 120Hz）、VRR（包括 AMD FreeSync Premium Pro）、杜比视界和 HDR10+ 游戏以及 ALLM。 还有一个游戏菜单，可以在其中调整亮度增强的设置。

声音方面，配备经过 Devial​​et 调校的 2.1.2 声道扬声器系统，总功率为 70W。 杜比全景声 (Dolby Atmos) 和 DTS: X 均受支持，并且有大量音频设置和预设模式可供深入研究。

UR8 使用哪种智能电视系统取决于您所在的地区。 在美国，您可以使用 Google TV，而在英国和澳大利亚，UR8 使用海信自己的 VIDAA 智能电视。 由于我居住在英国，因此我将讨论 VIDAA。 它支持大量应用程序，包括 Netflix 和 Prime Video 等热门应用程序，以及英国的 BBC iPlayer 和 ITVX。 它还支持英国的 Freely，可用于通过 Wi-Fi 观看直播、广播电视，无需卫星或天线连接。

  • 功能评分：4.5/5

海信UR8评测：画质

  • 出色的背光控制
  • 有效防眩光屏幕
  • 颜色不符合测量值

在亮度方面，UR8 达到了一些有趣的数字。 在电影制片人模式下，测得的 HDR 峰值亮度为 2,097 尼特，在标准模式下，达到 2,394 尼特。 这些都是可靠的结果，虽然三星 S99H 等旗舰 OLED 现在已经击败了这一点（它达到了 2,743 尼特峰值 HDR），但它确实击败了同价位的更多标准 mini-LED，例如三星 QN80H，我测得它的峰值 HDR 为 1,149 尼特（尽管这是在 55 英寸型号上）。

全屏 HDR 亮度也很稳定，在 Filmmaker 和标准模式下分别为 771 尼特和 767 尼特。 UR8 在 SDR 标准下提供了更令人印象深刻的亮度，其峰值亮度达到 1,514 尼特，全屏亮度达到 778 尼特。

不过，最令人惊讶的测量结果是 UR8 的 HDR 色域覆盖范围。 它不仅达到了 BT.2020 色彩空间的 95.1%，这是我迄今为止在电视上测得的最高值，而且它在 UHDA-P3 色彩空间中的色彩空间达到了惊人的 145.2%，这大大超过了我去年在三星 S95F 上使用相同色彩空间时所达到的 100% 的高点。

看到这些结果，我预计颜色会非常壮观 - 这引出了我对 UR8 的主要批评：我看到的颜色没有反映这些测量结果。 当我观看《Elemental》时，UR8 仍然呈现出强烈、鲜艳的色彩，例如 Ember 的火焰和 Wade 水的蓝色，但它们没有我所期待的流行。 在《爱乐之城》的春季派对上，米娅的黄色连衣裙看起来明亮自然，但我在其他电视上看到过更迷人的颜色。

我发现，当我将 UR8 与三星 QN80H（相同价格范围内的标准 mini-LED）进行比较时，QN80H 实际上提供了更大胆的色彩。 以同样的《爱乐之城》场景进行对比，米娅的黄色裙子、绿色的灌木丛以及一些参加聚会的人的红色服装在QN80H上看起来更加生动。 UR8 的颜色看起来很自然，但缺乏我对 RGB 电视所期望的令人惊叹的因素。

遗憾的是UR8的色彩没有我希望的那么耀眼，因为在其他方面，UR8也很出色，尤其是它的背光控制。 标准 mini-LED 电视确实可能会出现光晕现象（明亮物体发出的光在黑暗背景下会在该物体周围产生光晕效果），但 UR8 的情况并非如此，在大多数测试中，它几乎没有出现光晕现象。 从更极端的角度观看 UR8 确实发现了一些光晕，但它比我过去在一些迷你 LED 电视上看到的要好。

在观看《蝙蝠侠》时，UR8 也表现出了强烈的对比度，以深黑色调为主，明暗色调之间保持着良好的平衡，表现出蝙蝠侠在米斯塞尔市长家的犯罪现场或蝙蝠洞周围的明亮灯光下徘徊。 我确实注意到黑人在某些场景中可能呈现灰色色调，但在大多数情况下，蝙蝠侠看起来不错。

我确实发现杜比视界黑暗图像模式太暗，无法在明亮的房间里观看，尽管有防反射屏幕，但在环境和较暗的条件下效果很好。 更明亮的杜比视界 IQ 图像模式最适合明亮的房间。 如果您确实使用 Dolby Vision IQ，我建议将亮度从 50 降至 49，并关闭精确细节和超分辨率，以获得具有更好对比度的更自然的图像。

《异形：罗慕路斯》也有类似的故事。 UR8 出色地展示了太空场景，当宇航员接近文艺复兴空间站时，月光与太空的黑色形成了良好的对比。 太空的黑色偶尔会变成灰色，但对于迷你 LED 背光电视来说仍然非常好。 背光控制再次被证明是 UR8 的强项。

在所有 HDR 电影中，UR8 都能呈现清晰的纹理，以及人物、服装和物体的精致细节。 UR8 很好地展示了《异形：罗慕路斯》中采矿船上各种控制台的复杂纹理。 特写镜头也真实清晰地显示了汗水、毛发和皱纹等面部细节。

我确实发现奇怪的一件事是，对于非杜比视界内容，电影制片人、电影和 IMAX 增强图像模式看起来都相同。 亮度、颜色或对比度似乎没有真正的差异——这是我对电视的期望。

UR8在运动方面表现出色。 在 BBC iPlayer 上观看一些世界杯精彩片段时，在默认的体育画面模式下，动作非常流畅。 虽然大多数运动风格都有效，但我发现自己使用的是“清晰”或“标准”。 此模式下颜色增强器默认打开，我个人发现颜色过于饱和，所以我将其关闭，颜色看起来更自然。 我确实注意到，在非常快速的相机平移过程中，纹理会变得模糊，但在大多数情况下，UR8 非常适合运动。

  • 画质评分：4 / 5

海信UR8评测：音质

  • 2.1.2声道扬声器阵列
  • 良好的低音和准确性
  • 声场可能会很窄

UR8内置2.1.2声道扬声器阵列，由帝瓦雷调音，总功率70W。 有很多预设的声音模式和设置，但我主要使用标准和剧院模式进行测试。

在观看《蝙蝠侠》中企鹅追逐的场景时，UR8 提供了良好的低音水平，准确地传达了蝙蝠车引擎的隆隆声。 UR8 也表现出了良好的准确性，能够将轮胎转动的声音、子弹喷射的声音和过往车辆的喇叭声准确地映射到屏幕上的动作。

虽然我通常在大多数电视上使用剧院模式，但我发现 UR8 有时会变得刺眼，突然的亮度会分散我的注意力。 标准模式是一个非常合适的选择，虽然它没有剧院模式那么宽的声场，但它更容易控制。

UR8 整体上提供了扎实的声音，但我确实觉得它的声场很窄，这意味着并非蝙蝠侠场景的每个元素都有呼吸的空间。 对于电视来说，这是一个不错的音响系统，但总的来说，我仍然推荐一个条形音箱来搭配它。

  • 音质评分：4 / 5

海信UR8评测：设计

  • 坚固的结构
  • 实心底座
  • 深度稍大

UR8 具有实用且安全的设计。 当电视安装在中央底座上时，它本身感觉很坚固，尽管它是由塑料材料制成的，但它确实感觉很坚固。 这款电视比一些竞争对手（例如三星 QN80H）稍深一些，但同样感觉做工精良。

正如我上面提到的，UR8 具有防眩光屏幕，可以很好地限制明亮条件下的反射。 我测试的 65 英寸型号就其尺寸而言感觉很轻，并且有一个装饰边框，尽管底部边框比顶部和侧面的边框厚。 连接位于电视背面的侧面，方便连接。

UR8 配备了海信自己的 USB-C 和太阳能充电遥控器，对我来说这是市场上更好的控制器之一。 它确实感觉有点轻，但对我来说，按钮布局很合乎逻辑，而且很高兴看到更便宜的电视配备可充电遥控器。

  • 设计得分：4 / 5

海信 UR8 评测：智能电视和菜单

  • Google TV 美国、VIDAA 英国和澳大利亚
  • 良好的图像和音频设置
  • 过时的外观

由于我居住在英国，因此我将讨论 UR8 中采用的 VIDAA 智能电视平台（也用于澳大利亚型号）。 如果您位于美国，UR8 将使用 Google TV 作为其智能电视平台。

VIDAA 是一个可维护的智能电视系统。 它支持大量主要应用程序，包括 Netflix、Disney Plus 和 Prime Video，以及英国广播公司的应用程序，包括 BBC iPlayer 和 ITVX。 主屏幕提供了大量内容推荐，但屏幕顶部还有一个很大的广告横幅空间，这可能会分散注意力。

菜单布局整齐、逻辑性强，大多数设置都很容易找到。 浏览这些菜单时的响应时间也很好。 有很多用于调整图像和声音的设置，尽管我没有使用很多。

然而，VIDAA 看起来确实有点过时，尤其是在菜单中。 它没有三星 Tizen 或 Google TV 的时尚，也没有 Roku 的简洁和色彩。 其次，对于经常更改设置的人来说，每次都会弹出生态警告，这可能会令人沮丧；并且似乎没有办法将其关闭。

  • 智能电视得分：3.5或4

海信 UR8 评测：游戏

  • 近乎全套的功能
  • 11.7ms 输入延迟（正确设置）
  • 最高支持 4K 180Hz 刷新率

UR8 实际上非常适合游戏。 它具有四个 HDMI 2.1 端口，支持高达 180Hz 的 4K（支持控制台的 4K 120Hz）、VRR（包括 FreeSync Premium Pro）、杜比视界和 HDR10+ 游戏以及 ALLM。

为了获得最低的输入延迟时间（我在 4K 60Hz 下测量为 11.7 毫秒），您确实必须进行一些设置。 将 UR8 置于游戏模式后，我必须打开刷新率功能，该功能优先考虑更快的帧速率，这就是我得到上述结果的方法。 在不调整这些设置的情况下，我测得输入延迟时间为 20 毫秒，高于我们在测试中寻找的 15 毫秒阈值。

在 4K 120Hz 下玩《战地 V》，实际游戏感觉很流畅，UR8 很好地处理了快速移动的动作序列，比如沙漠任务中的枪战。 整体图像质量良好，亮度高、色彩大胆、对比度强。 我确实注意到，在特别快速的相机平移过程中，某些纹理可能会变得模糊，但这种情况并非每次都会发生。

  • 游戏评分：4.5/5

海信UR8评测：价值

  • 在美国和澳大利亚物超所值
  • 在英国价格过高
  • 总体来说性价比不错

价值是海信 UR8 的一个很难评价的属性。 由于 RGB mini-LED 仍处于起步阶段（2025 年才推出，今年才首次出现在较小的屏幕上），我确实预计 RGB 电视会很昂贵，甚至是像 UR8 这样的入门级型号。

有了 UR8，一切都取决于您所在的位置。 当它发售时，你可以在美国以 1,499 美元的价格购买 65 英寸型号，而且价格只会下降。 这使得 UR8 在价格上与标准 mini-LED 直接竞争，为寻找该价格范围内电视的人们提供了更多选择。 它在澳大利亚也很划算，65 英寸的售价为 2,495 澳元，约合 1,799 美元/1,299 英镑。 我预计澳大利亚的价格也会很快下降。

不幸的是，英国的情况却并非如此。 最近推出的 65 英寸显示屏售价为 2,299 英镑，实际上比 LG C6 OLED 更贵——虽然 RGB 旨在成为 OLED 的直接竞争对手，正如我所提到的，但它还没有实现。 我在一些零售商处看到 UR8 降到了 1,999 英镑，但这仍然是 OLED 级别的定价。

总体而言，UR8 确实物有所值。 它具有良好的功能集，提供不错的内置声音，并且非常适合游戏，虽然图像没有完全达到我的期望，但与大多数 mini-LED 相比，它仍然很稳定。 遗憾的是，价值主张取决于地区。

  • 价值得分：4 / 5

我如何测试海信 UR8

  • 经过两周多的测试
  • 在实验室不同光照条件下进行测试
  • 使用 Portrait Displays 的 Calman 色彩校准软件进行测量

我测试海信 UR8 的第一步是为关键测试建立最佳图像模式，然后我选择了电影制片人模式和影院模式（不可否认，它们看起来非常相似）。

然后我使用参考场景来测试 UR8 的图像质量，重点是亮度、颜色、细节、升级、对比度和背光控制。 我使用了几个相同的场景来测试电视的内置扬声器。

我还使用 Xbox Series X 来测试电视的游戏功能和性能，玩《战地 V》。

除了客观测试之外，我还使用专用设备对 UR8 进行了测量。 其中包括 Jeti Spctral 15VA 光谱辐射计和 Klein K-10A 色度计（两种仪表一起配置），以及 Murideo Six G 8K Metal 测试图案生成器。 我使用 Portrait Displays 的 Calman 色彩校准软件进行了测量。

我进行的第一个测量是 UR8 在 SDR 和 HDR 下的亮度。 我使用了尺寸范围为 1-100% 的白色窗口图案，其中峰值 (10%) 和全屏 (100%) 窗口作为主要焦点。 我在 UR8 的标准和电影制作模式图片模式下进行了测量。

之后，我测量了颜色和灰度精度（以 SDR 为单位），重点关注 Delta-E 值（发送的测试信号与屏幕上显示的信号之间的误差范围）。

接下来，我测量了 UR8 的 HDR 色域覆盖范围，重点关注 BT.2020 和 UHDA-P3 色彩空间。

我还测量了 UR8 的 HDR EOTF（1,000、4,000 和 10,000 尼特）。 这显示了 UR8 在亮光和暗光级别的准确度。 我还测试了 UR8 的光谱功率分布，它展示了色彩性能。

最后，我使用 Leo Bodnar 4K HDMi 输入延迟测试仪测试了 UR8 的输入延迟时间。
